order_confound_rule: a state whose ONLY inter-arm difference is a `timeout` on the SECOND arm, while the arms ran in the frozen sequential order under the shared per-state allowance, is classified as ORDER_ATTRIBUTABLE.  Its V2 difference is reported but may NOT be read as a scorer mechanism advantage: the second arm was charged for time it did not spend.  A `timeout` on the FIRST arm is never order-attributable.  Every affected state keeps its record and stays in the 64-state denominator; none is dropped, replaced or re-run.

O2 a state where the SECOND arm is cheap: BOTH arms complete (baseline for the pair)

detail.what_changed_between_O2_and_O3: ONLY which arm ran first.  The state, the mask, the ordered legal lists, the scorers' own cost and both call ceilings are identical, so O3 is an instrument effect.

rows.name: O3 the SAME state with a SLOW FIRST arm and a FAST SECOND arm: the SECOND arm times out -- the second arm paid for time the first arm spent

loss_of_comparability_case.reading: NOT_COMPARABLE means exactly "no usable first step existed on both arms"; it is NOT a difference between the scorers

detail.why: a scorer is a pure function of its step state, so the first call either happens or it does not; it is never different because another arm ran earlier

v1_order_invariance_statement: V1 compares the first step, and no scorer call precedes it, so the second arm has spent nothing and no deadline can have fired.  V1 is order-invariant by construction, and the O4 counterexample confirms it by running the same state under two different first arms.
v2_order_sensitivity_statement: V2 compares per-arm completion, which is exactly what the shared deadline bounds, so a second-arm `timeout` may be caused by the order rather than by the scorer.  O2 and O3 are the counterexample pair: only the identity of the first arm changed.
